body.heading: A game you can price exactly
paragraphs: Here is a simple game: you pay 1 coin to play, flip a fair coin, and win 2 coins if it lands heads. Half the time you gain, half the time you lose. Your average winnings per play are 0.5 x 2 = 1 coin - exactly what you paid. Games where the average payout equals the price are called fair.

That average is the game's expected value. It does not predict any single play; it describes what happens over many plays. Play the coin game a thousand times and your total will hover near break-even, wandering a little but always pulled back toward the average.

body.heading: Pricing a dice game
paragraphs: Now roll a die and win that many coins: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6, each equally likely. The expected payout is the average of the faces, 3.5 coins. If a stall charges 4 coins to play, you lose about half a coin per game on average - play 100 games and you can expect to be roughly 50 coins down. If it charges 3, the edge flips to you.

This is precisely how carnival games and lotteries are priced: the price sits a little above the expected payout, so the stall profits slowly and reliably while individual players mostly have fun and occasionally win. Nothing is rigged - the arithmetic does all the work, in plain sight.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Invent a game with three outcomes - for example, draw a card: red pays 2, a face card pays 5, anything else pays nothing. Work out the expected payout by multiplying each prize by its probability and adding the results. (There are 26 red cards in 52, and 12 face cards, of which 6 are also red - take care not to count those twice.)

Then set what you think is a fair price, and test it with play money over 50 rounds. Watching your paper fortune drift toward the prediction is the moment expected value stops being a formula and becomes a feeling.

takeaway: Multiply each prize by its probability and add them up - that is a game's expected value, and comparing it with the price tells you who the game favours.
